34
 the Netherlands,
35
 Cyprus,
36
 the Czech Republic,
37
 Chile
38
 and the United States.
23
 Equine dysautonomia affects all equids, with cases reported in donkeys,
16
 mules,
23
 zebras
17
 and horses.
29
, 
36

Comprehensive reviews of the clinical signs of EGS have been performed elsewhere.
15
, 
39
 Briefly, key clinical signs of EGS can include intestinal impaction, GI stasis, tachycardia, depression or lethargy, muscle tremors, hypersalivation, weight loss, drooping of the eyelids (ptosis) and rhinitis sicca.
39
 Expression of these clinical signs varies across the three clinical subcategories: acute, subacute and chronic.
40
 EGS is a devastating disease, with acute and subacute cases having a 100% mortality rate, with animals being euthanased for welfare reasons. Moreover, chronic cases are also associated with a 50% mortality rate.
40
 However, presentation of clinical signs can be highly variable between cases, and anecdotal evidence has suggested that, if the attending veterinarian is unfamiliar with EGS, it may be misdiagnosed as impaction colic, which does not respond to treatment (anecdotal personal communication with numerous veterinarians).

A standard clinical biomarker or assessment has yet to be identified for EGS, despite many clinicopathological investigations into potential serum biomarkers specific to EGS. It is noted that serum amyloid A and fibrinogen are elevated
41
; however, these are non‐specific inflammatory markers that are also elevated in colic, pneumonia, arthritis and other equine diseases.
42
 Differences in serum amino acid levels have been reported in the serum of horses with EGS when compared to healthy controls, with cases showing significantly higher taurine and decreased arginine, citrulline, cysteine, histidine, isoleucine, leucine, methionine, threonine, tyrosine and valine. However, this may reflect the dehydration, inappetence and malnutrition that is generally present in horses with EGS.
34
 Currently, the primary means of definitive diagnosis is via full‐tissue thickness biopsy of the ileum or gustatory papillae
43
 to assess neuronal damage via histopathology.

Over the past century, many authors have reviewed the neuropathology of EGS. Damage to neurons of the PNS occurs in the paravertebral ganglia, prevertebral ganglia, dorsal root ganglia, ciliary ganglia and ENS,
38
, 
44
, 
45
 although the extent of neuronal damage and loss varies between cases. Pathological changes, including central chromatolysis, loss of Nissl substance, eccentric pyknotic nuclei and occasional cytoplasmic vacuoles, have been reported in neurons of both the ENS and PNS.
38
, 
46
 In acute EGS, these changes are present most extensively in the ileum in the submucosal plexus, followed by the myenteric plexus, with subsequent extension to the nearest ganglia. In chronic EGS, these changes extend to other regions of the ENS and PNS.
47
 A study published in 1988 investigated neuronal damage in the CNS of EGS cases and observed minor neuronal depletion across several brain regions; however, these changes were also observed in the CNS of a horse with laminitis, leading the authors to suggest that the CNS changes observed in EGS are non‐specific.
44
 CNS pathology was revisited in 2001 by Hahn et al.,
48
 who investigated the extent of neuronal degeneration in the cranial nerves (CNs), brain regions and spinal cord of acute, subacute and chronic EGS cases. They reported affected neurons in the general somatic efferent nucleus of CNIII (oculomotor nerve) and CNVII (facial nerve), the nucleus of CNVI (abducens nerve) and CNXII (hypoglossal nerve) and the motor nucleus of CNV (trigeminal nerve). More recently, an investigation into the neuromuscular junction (NMJ) of synapses in muscle fibres from EGS cases, compared with control horses and a single unconfirmed botulism case, claimed that there were distinct differences, suggesting that this ruled out botulism as a causal agent.
49
 Using electron microscopy, this study noted ultrastructural abnormalities, and suggested endocytosis of synaptic vesicles was inhibited or disrupted in the EGS NMJs.

Further studies have observed damage to organs other than the GI tract. In 2000, Perkins et al.
50
 reported damage to the neurons in the parasympathetic terminal cardiac ganglia of the heart. These neurons showed identical pathology to neurons in the PNS, with chromatolysis and vacuolation of cytoplasm. Perkins et al.
50
 also observed changes in heart rate variability, suggestive of a reduction in cardiac autonomic control. In 2001, Marrs et al.
51
 investigated previous reports of damage to the liver,
46
 and their results suggested that some EGS cases are associated with steatosis (accumulation of cellular lipids) and lymphocyte infiltration into the portal areas of the liver.
51
 It remains to be determined whether this damage is the effect of a specific causal agent or a result of altered lipid metabolism associated with anorexia, general disruption to PNS signalling to the liver, or a secondary or concurrent infection.

Combined, these findings suggest that neurons in the ENS, SANS and PANS are all affected in EGS.

The risk factors for EGS are the most well studied of the animal dysautonomias, with published research covering soil and pasture composition, mycobiome, weather patterns, equine management and nutrition.

Soil composition has been investigated as a risk factor for EGS. Edwards et al.
52
 performed a longitudinal study across 23 sites with known EGS cases and 11 control sites, sampling soils to measure mineral composition. They observed that sites with previous cases of EGS showed significantly higher soil iron, lead and chromium, and significantly lower mercury.
52
 Another study, by Wylie et al.,
53
 suggested that EGS sites were associated with increased titanium and decreased zinc when their results were compared to one database, and higher titanium and lower chromium when compared to another database. However, this study reported difficulty in the interpretation of results due to complexities in the reference databases. It also acknowledged the limitations of associating soil composition analysis with EGS due to the wide and complex number of factors influencing the uptake of minerals by plants and animals.

Perhaps unsurprisingly given its name, herbage as a risk factor for EGS has also been investigated. The longitudinal study previously mentioned
52
 also performed botanical surveys and collected samples for analysis of plants on EGS‐associated pastures. They found buttercups (Ranunculus sp.) were highly prevalent on EGS pastures, and analysis of these found significantly increased levels of ranunculin, a protein produced by all Ranunculaceae, which is broken down into protoanemonin, a toxin known to be harmful to equids.
54
 In 2011, the influence of Ranunculus species on EGS was directly investigated by Michl et al.,
55
 who observed significantly higher levels of ranunculin in Ranunculus repens samples collected from EGS‐associated pastures compared to control pastures. However, it is noted that buttercup species are widespread and common in the UK between April and October,
56
 which means that they are usually present in equine grazing pastures whether EGS develops or not, and the authors themselves state it is unlikely that consumption of Ranunculus species alone was the sole cause of EGS.

McGorum et al.
57
 investigated the mycobiome of horses with EGS to determine if a mycotoxin produced by fungi may be responsible for the disease.
57
 By analysing the GI microbiota of 54 EGS and 48 non‐EGS co‐grazers, which were on the same field as horses that died of EGS, plus 67 control horses, the authors identified 56 key phylotypes that showed variation in the EGS gut compared to that of control horses, many of which were capable of producing mycotoxins. However, this study did not confirm if any of these fungi were actively producing these mycotoxins, or if they contributed to the associated pathology of EGS. This study serves as a basis for future studies into these questions.

It has long been anecdotally observed by veterinarians and horse owners familiar with EGS that there is an association between weather patterns and the occurrence of EGS. Wylie et al.
58
 found an increased risk of EGS during periods with more frost days and increasing sunlight hours in horses in Scotland, and a decreased risk associated with consistently higher maximum temperature. This likely reflects the changes from spring (when the weather is more variable with more frost days) and summer (when the temperature remains more consistently high). This is consistent with findings from multiple sources that report the highest incidence in Spring (April and May).
31
, 
53
, 
58
, 
59
, 
60

Feline dysautonomia (FD) (or Key‒Gaskell syndrome) was first reported in 1982 in the UK
61
 and has since been reported in Belgium,
62
 France,
24
 Denmark,
27
 Switzerland,
63
 the United States,
64
 Brazil
65
 and New Zealand.
66

Clinical signs of FD include dilated pupils with lack of pupillary light response (PLR), protrusion of the nictitating membrane (third eyelid) and dry mucosal membranes. Vomiting, regurgitation and anorexia or inappetence are common, with one study of 40 cats reporting anorexia in all of the animals in the study.
14
 These clinical signs occur alongside occasional GI stasis, constipation or diarrhoea. Other less common clinical signs include dysuria, bradycardia, nasal congestion or discharge, and loss of anal tone.
14
 Onset of these clinical signs ranges from acute (days) to chronic (weeks), and the prognosis is generally poor. Weight loss was more frequently observed in more chronic cases. Despite high mortality rates, FD has the highest survival rate of the dysautonomias described in this review, with reported survival rates of up to 30% and near complete recovery within 12 months in survivors.
14
 However, survival rates may not be directly comparable between species, given the relative ease and cost of treating different species.

Of those studies that reported blood or serum biochemistry, the majority noted no abnormal observations,
64
 with others citing mildly increased urea and globulins, which the authors suggest is likely indicative of dehydration.
64
, 
67
, 
68

Pathological changes reported in FD include depletion of neurons in autonomic ganglia (dorsal root ganglia, coeliac‐mesenteric ganglia and cranial cervical ganglion) and the submucosal and myenteric plexus of the ileum, duodenum, jejunum, cecum and colon.
64
, 
65
 Neurons are reported as being chromatolytic with loss of Nissl substance and ribosomes, eccentric pyknotic or karyorrhexic nuclei and occasional vacuoles.
69
 Both pre‐ and postganglionic neurons of the PANS and SANS are affected. Inflammation or gliosis is rarely reported; however, there are sporadic cases in which infiltration of lymphocytes to the ANS has been reported.
14
, 
61
, 
64

A comprehensive analysis of the risk factors associated with FD has not been conducted; however, a study of 40 cases
70
 suggested that there was no significant difference between urban and rural cases. This study also showed that FD affects cats both with and without outdoor access, suggesting that the etiological agent was not exclusively accessible outdoors. Younger animals appear more predisposed to FD, with the average age of onset being approximately 2 years old.
64
, 
71
 No studies have stated any difference in the diagnosis of FD in males or females, suggesting this disease, like the other dysautonomias discussed in this review, is not sex linked.

FD has been associated with Clostridium botulinum, the bacterium responsible for botulism, via its production of a potent neurotoxin. A 2004 study
72
 into an outbreak of FD in a closed, indoor colony of cats found significantly increased immunoglobulin A against C. botulinum in the FD cases compared with controls. When samples of the animals' dry food were tested, they too tested positive for C. botulinum, suggesting the outbreak may have been linked to contaminated food.

Canine dysautonomia (CD) was first reported in England in 1983
73
 as a disease with striking similarities to FD. Since the original report, the disease has been reported in Scotland,
74
 Germany,
75
 Greece,
76
 Canada
77
 and the USA.
78
, 
79
 While the majority of recent cases appear to be from the USA (usually the Midwest of the country), this may be due to increased awareness resulting in increased diagnosis, rather than reflecting the true prevalence, as the available publications are from the University of Wyoming,
78
 the University of Missouri
13
, 
80
 and the Kansas State University.
79
 It is therefore unknown if CD is observed or reported in other states in the USA.

The clinical signs of CD are almost identical to FD. The most common signs across several studies are vomiting, loss of PLR (exhibiting mydriasis), dysuria and diarrhoea with a consistent absence or decrease of anal tone.
79
, 
81
 Lethargy and protrusion of the nictitating membranes are also frequently reported. Occasionally, constipation or GI hypomotility, dry mucosal membranes and nasal congestion have been observed.
74
, 
75

Postmortem analysis of ANS tissue has shown neuron loss in the cranial cervical, coeliac‐mesenteric, pelvic and ciliary ganglia, submucosal and myenteric plexus of the GI tract and brainstem.
78
, 
81
, 
82
 All ganglia, brain stem and ENS neurons showed identical patterns of degeneration. Additionally, several studies reported degeneration in the ventral horn of the spinal cord, which may be indicative of damage to motor neurons. Indeed, two studies in a small number of dogs reported clinical signs of muscular abnormalities such as severe muscle weakness and wasting, hindlimb paresis and muscle tremors.
83
, 
84

Within affected ganglia of both the SANS and PANS, neuron numbers were reduced, with remaining neurons appearing eosinophilic due to a lack of Nissl substance, with karyorrhectic or pyknotic nuclei. Some neurons contained diffuse vacuoles around the cytoplasm, some of which contained eosinophilic material.
85
 Gliosis is recorded in several studies, and one study reported infiltration of lymphocytes, macrophages and plasma cells in a small number of cases.
85

No degeneration of the cerebellum, midbrain, hippocampus or vagal sympathetic trunk has been reported in CD.
85

CD, similar to other animal dysautonomias, is mainly observed in younger animals, with an average age at onset of approximately 2 years old.
79
, 
83

Berghaus et al.
80
 evaluated the risk factors for CD in Missouri, finding several correlations among the 30 cases examined. First was the season, with April being the month with the highest incidence, followed by February and January, and a smaller peak in November and December. A second study, covering 65 cases in the UK,
85
 reported that the majority of CD cases occurred in February and March, followed by May, then April and July. In contrast, a more recent study,
79
 which combined records from 79 dogs diagnosed with CD at the Kansas State University Veterinary Health Center between 2004 and 2021, found March, May and September had the highest numbers of reported cases. It may, then, be better stated that spring is the highest risk season, followed by autumn, rather than specific months. Given the variance in weather patterns between the Midwestern USA and the UK, it seems more likely that the seasonal change in weather induces a shift—either in the environment (flora or microbe growth) or within the animal—which is associated with the onset of dysautonomia.

Berghaus et al.
80
 also observed that rural dogs appeared to be more likely to contract CD (as did Harkin et al.
85
), particularly if those dogs were kept exclusively outdoors. Of note, there were no cases of CD where the dog was kept exclusively indoors. Dogs younger than 36 months were at highest risk, and correlations were observed with animals that had contact with cattle or pasture, drank water from farm ponds or had access to undeveloped land, such as woodlands. The authors also noted that many of the CD cases had reportedly consumed some form of wildlife and suggested that this may be the link between dysautonomia in herbivores and carnivores.

Leporine dysautonomia (LD) is suspected to be the same disease as rabbit mucoid enteropathy (RME) since it shares many of the same clinical signs.
86
 Indeed, in 1996, dysautonomia was confirmed in RME.
87
 Of particular interest is that LD has been confirmed in hares present in the same fields as horses diagnosed with dysautonomia,
18
 with these hares found dead after an EGS case. LD has been reported only in the UK
19
 and Croatia,
88
 although a report on mortality in farmed hares in Italy suggested pathological findings consistent with LD.
87

Clinical signs of LD are less well characterised than those of dysautonomias in other species due to the animals generally being found dead rather than undergoing treatment by a veterinarian. The cases that are observed are usually from domestic rabbit farms and present with emaciation (suggestive of anorexia or inappetence), distention of the abdomen and bladder (suggestive of dysuria) and lethargy.
89

The most recent report of LD is from 2022.
88
 Neurodegeneration was observed within the submucosal and myenteric plexus of the GI tract, with neurons noted as being swollen with vacuolated cytoplasm and pyknotic nuclei. The animal was found dead, and no clinical history was given.

Risk factors for LD have not been formally studied or published.

Two confirmed cases of dysautonomia have also been reported in New World camelids—one llama and one alpaca.

Dysautonomia of camelids was first reported in 2006 in Missouri,
20
 with the deaths of two llamas. The first llama had presented with similar clinical signs, but no examination was performed after the animal was found dead in the pasture 5 days prior to the second llama developing clinical signs. The second llama exhibited weight loss, GI stasis and obstruction (measured by lack of GI sounds), fixed dilated pupils with no PLR, loss of anal tone and dysuria. The animal was euthanased due to its deteriorating condition. Histopathology identified severe neuronal degeneration in the iliac, right ciliary and cranial mesenteric ganglia, the oesophagus, colon and lungs. The few surviving neurons were hypereosinophilic and vacuolated. Of note, this llama was also diagnosed with a multidrug‐resistant strain of Salmonella enterica serovar Agona. This coinfection was thought to be responsible for the inflammatory responses throughout the GI tract. Both llamas shared a pasture with horses, none of which exhibited any clinical signs of EGS.

The second case of dysautonomia in a camelid was reported in an alpaca in 2009, also in Missouri.
21
 The alpaca presented with anorexia, lethargy, weight loss, muscle tremors and absent GI sounds. In this case, the PLR was normal and there was no ptosis. Following 3 days of treatment (fluid therapy, an enema and administration of flunixin meglamine [NSAID] and ceftiofur hydrochloride [a cephalosporin antibiotic]), the animal was euthanased. Histopathology found neurodegeneration in cranial mesenteric ganglia and themyenteric plexus of the large intestine, with neurons described as hypereosinophilic with pyknotic nuclei, and occasional cytoplasmic vacuoles were observed. This alpaca had fence line contact with two horses, although no other animals on the pasture or surrounding premises were affected.

Finally, a publication in 2004
22
 drew similarities between abomasal emptying defect (AED) of sheep and dysautonomia. AED results in distention and impaction of the abomasum, with a poor prognosis for the animal. In this study, histopathology of ganglia was performed, showing swelling of neuronal processes, chromatolysis and vacuolation of some neurons. Based on the lack of inflammation, neuronal pathology and previous reports of heart arrythmia in AED, the authors suggested that this too was a form of dysautonomia.

---

[CLINICAL PRESENTATION ACROSS SPECIES]
Given the marked similarity in PNS pathology of neurons across species affected with dysautonomia, it seems plausible that there is a shared aetiological agent despite the broad differences in species discussed here.

Some of the differences in clinical presentation between EGS and LD, and CD and FD are easily explained by differences in physical anatomy. Horses and rabbits are incapable of vomiting due to tight gastric sphincters,
90
 unlike cats and dogs, who are capable of vomiting. This inability to vomit therefore results in excessive gastric reflux via the nasal passages in horses and rabbits, but not in cats and dogs.

Similarly, while horses can sweat across their entire body, cats and dogs have limited ability to sweat across the fur‐covered areas of their bodies and so are limited to sweating from hairless areas such as the digital pads. This makes a clinical observation of ‘patchy sweating’ considerably more difficult to identify and diagnose in dogs and cats, which may explain the absence of reported changes in sweat patterns in cats and dogs with dysautonomia.

In horses, loss of sympathetic signalling to Muller's superior tarsal muscle results in ptosis of the upper eyelid.
91
 The same syndrome in cats results primarily in protrusion of the third eyelid, as cats have smooth muscle innervation within the third eyelid.
92
 Dogs lack sympathetic innervation of the third eyelid, which may explain the rarity of nictitating membrane protrusion associated with CD.
93

While the majority of research focuses on the clinical signs and pathology in the GI tract of dysautonomia cases, the effect of damage to the PNS is also occasionally observed in the cardiovascular system. Equids with EGS consistently exhibit tachycardia, while dogs and cats exhibit bradycardia when experiencing dysautonomia. This is likely due to the difference in control of heart rate between equids and carnivores, but may also reflect differences in the extent of sympathetic versus parasympathetic neurons between species, given the opposing nature of these PNS subsets, although a comparative study of neurodegeneration within the PNS of these species would be required to confirm this.

---

[DISCUSSION]
Given the marked similarity in PNS pathology of neurons across species affected with dysautonomia, it seems plausible that there is a shared aetiological agent despite the broad differences in species discussed here.

Some of the differences in clinical presentation between EGS and LD, and CD and FD are easily explained by differences in physical anatomy. Horses and rabbits are incapable of vomiting due to tight gastric sphincters,
90
 unlike cats and dogs, who are capable of vomiting. This inability to vomit therefore results in excessive gastric reflux via the nasal passages in horses and rabbits, but not in cats and dogs.

Similarly, while horses can sweat across their entire body, cats and dogs have limited ability to sweat across the fur‐covered areas of their bodies and so are limited to sweating from hairless areas such as the digital pads. This makes a clinical observation of ‘patchy sweating’ considerably more difficult to identify and diagnose in dogs and cats, which may explain the absence of reported changes in sweat patterns in cats and dogs with dysautonomia.

In horses, loss of sympathetic signalling to Muller's superior tarsal muscle results in ptosis of the upper eyelid.
91
 The same syndrome in cats results primarily in protrusion of the third eyelid, as cats have smooth muscle innervation within the third eyelid.
92
 Dogs lack sympathetic innervation of the third eyelid, which may explain the rarity of nictitating membrane protrusion associated with CD.
93

While the majority of research focuses on the clinical signs and pathology in the GI tract of dysautonomia cases, the effect of damage to the PNS is also occasionally observed in the cardiovascular system. Equids with EGS consistently exhibit tachycardia, while dogs and cats exhibit bradycardia when experiencing dysautonomia. This is likely due to the difference in control of heart rate between equids and carnivores, but may also reflect differences in the extent of sympathetic versus parasympathetic neurons between species, given the opposing nature of these PNS subsets, although a comparative study of neurodegeneration within the PNS of these species would be required to confirm this.

Risk factors for dysautonomia have been studied most extensively in EGS and CD, where there appears to be some overlap in seasonal disposition, and in EGS, CD and FD, where younger animals appear to be at higher risk.

Besides the similar clinical presentation and pathology, there are similarities in the time of year that the majority of dysautonomia cases occur. Both CD and EGS show a significant increase in case numbers in the spring, a season marked by significant changes in plant metabolism, temperature fluctuations, extending daylight hours and turbulent weather. Each of these has the potential to influence bacterial and fungal growth,
94
 diet, circadian rhythm
95
 and pathogen exposure.
96
 Studying this seasonal disposition is therefore a profoundly complex web to untangle.

It has been shown that dogs in rural areas that spent more, or all, of their time outdoors were significantly more likely to contract CD.
80
 This aligns with EGS, as affected horses are kept primarily outdoors and almost always in rural areas. Horses are also regularly ‘turned out’ to pasture in the spring after being stabled through the winter. Berghaus et al. also reported that, in 52% of CD cases, the dog had fed on wildlife such as rabbits or birds (although the species ingested was not specified), further suggesting that this may act as a bridge between herbivorous ‘grass sickness’ and carnivores. However, given the large difference in diet between horses and dogs, it could also be suggested that the exposure comes from an environmental agent associated with rural environments. This could include agents from the soil rather than ingested material, which may also align with the seasonal disposition, given the increased growth rate of plants in spring and summer and the associated development of bacteria and fungi. However, FD was found to have no correlation with rural or urban environments,
14
 with several reported cases in animals kept exclusively indoors,
67
 which may suggest either a difference in causal agent or an agent accessed via contaminated feed.
72

Other studies investigating the microbiome and immune function of dysautonomia do not take season or weather into account in their analysis, perhaps fairly, given the complexity of such analysis. However, many publications have hypothesised that the causal agent is a fungus or microbe found in pasture, which increases its prevalence in the spring.
53
, 
57
, 
58
 Dogs, horses, hares, rabbits, llamas and outdoor‐kept cats would potentially be exposed to this pathogen either through direct consumption of the grass or through consuming herbivores that were previously exposed.

It is of note that studies into risk factors for dysautonomia in species other than horses do not account for the weather patterns leading up to the onset of clinical signs. While this is a relatively recent area of study in EGS, it appears likely that the weather plays some role in EGS onset and therefore may also play a role in dysautonomia of other species.

Both CD and EGS have reported cases of ‘outbreaks’, where multiple animals kept under the same conditions have died in rapid succession.

One outbreak of EGS was reported in Prezwalski's horses, resulting in the death of six out of eight horses in a herd.
97
 The horses were moved to a new pasture, and then 23 days later, the first horse showed clinical signs of acute EGS, being euthanased 48 hours later. Within 24 hours of the first case, five more horses developed acute EGS and were also euthanased. It is not noted if these animals were related, so any genetic predisposition is unclear. However, in this case, the instigating factor appears to have been the move to a new pasture.

The genetic component of EGS was investigated in 2020 by Vincze et al.,
98
 who examined genomic datasets from 1233 horses, 49 of which contracted EGS (3.97% prevalence). They found that certain stallions displayed a significantly higher risk for their descendants to develop EGS. The authors suggested a possible X‐linked inheritance but were unable to confirm this in their study.

There are similar reports of outbreaks of CD in related dogs. The most recent occurred in a litter of five Havanese puppies in Missouri, in 2015.
78
 Four puppies had accessed an outdoor yard, which had new topsoil applied 6 months prior and evidence of construction work on‐site, for a less than 5‐minute period. Within 16 days, all four puppies developed vomiting and other signs of CD, and they were euthanased within 9 days of the onset of clinical signs. The breeder of the puppies had nine other dogs on the property with regular access to the yard that remained unaffected. Postmortem examination of the euthanased puppies showed widespread motor neuron degeneration in the ventral horn of the spinal cord, but the DRG was unaffected. The authors did not establish if this was a coincidence or evidence of horizontal transmission and suggested that the most likely cause was exposure to a soil‐borne pathogen or toxic agent.

A similar outbreak occurred in 2002,
99
 where four German shorthaired pointer puppies from the same litter developed clinical signs consistent with dysautonomia shortly after their dam was euthanased for CD. Unlike the outbreak described above, these puppies had no access to the outdoors and were all confirmed to be positive for canine parvovirus. There were two other adult dogs on the property that did not develop CD. The diet of these two dogs was different to that of the puppies’ dam; the dam was being fed commercial puppy food that was of a different brand and formulation to that fed to the other two dogs. While it is possible that this puppy food, fed to only the affected animals, was contaminated with a neurotoxic agent, there were many other variables in this case that the authors did not discuss.
99

The role of specific genes in dyautonomia of any species remains unclear, highlighting the requirement for further research.

In 1966, an antibiotic called salinomycin was identified as the primary cause of an outbreak of dysautonomia in cats.
100
, 
101
 This drug has known toxicity to neurons, particularly in horses,
102
 dogs and cats,
100
, 
101
 but is commonly used in broiler hens as a coccidiostatic treatment. It is assumed that after treatment of the chickens, the drug remained active and contaminated the cat food due to improper handling. This outbreak showed overlap with FD in terms of clinical presentation and pathology.

Salinomycin belongs to the ionophore group of antibiotics, which reversibly transport ions through cell membranes, disrupting membrane potential. Ionophore poisoning in horses, cats and dogs shows overlap with dysautonomia in some clinical presentations. In horses, overlapping clinical signs between EGS and ionophore poisoning are colic, anorexia, lethargy, weakness, sweating and distension of the bladder for acute cases, plus weight loss and lethargy in chronic cases. However, additional clinical signs in ionophore poisoning cases include severe cardiac arrythmias, oedema, diarrhoea, polyuria, myoglobinuria and respiratory distress, which are rarely seen in EGS.
102
, 
103
 In cats, clinical signs of ionophore poisoning are more strongly associated with diminished spinal reflex resulting in hindlimb paralysis,
101
 something that was not frequently observed in FD cases.
14
, 
64
, 
71
 Additionally, histopathological examination of tissues from ionophore poisoning cases showed severe vacuolation in dorsal root ganglia neurons and severe degeneration of muscle cells,
104
, 
105
 which are not observed in dysautonomia to the same extent.

It seems likely that primary ionophore toxicity may cause dysautonomia in some cases, but this is likely to be a discrete syndrome rather than the main cause of the cases reported here. Such contamination would also result in sudden widespread outbreak reports resulting from distribution of the contaminated feed across the market, as was the case in 1966, where an outbreak occurred in the Netherlands and Switzerland due to contamination of two brands of dry cat food with salinomycin.
100
 Therefore, ionophore poisoning is unlikely to be the primary cause of dysautonomia.

One of the key challenges in dysautonomia studies is consistent access to samples, tissues and metadata from cases of dysautonomia, as well as matched control animals, so that meaningful comparisons can be made between cases. It is here that biobanks present a significant opportunity. The Equine Grass Sickness Fund (EGSF, www.grasssickness.org.uk/) owns a biobank of EGS samples, including formalin‐fixed tissues, faeces, urine, blood and saliva from EGS‐diagnosed horses and soil from corresponding pasture. The EGSF also collects case reports from veterinarians and horse owners who have encountered a case of EGS, even when samples have not been submitted to the biobank. This reporting has allowed tracking of cases throughout the years, leading to better understanding of the prevalence and risk factors of the disease. A similar reporting platform and biobank for dysautonomia in other species would be invaluable for advancing our understanding of how these diseases develop and for the identification of potential risk factors.

The causative agent of dysautonomia remains elusive, but we do know that some species exhibit neuronal damage in particular anatomical regions of the PNS while others do not. Comparative pathology across the entire PNS of each species should be performed to allow comparison of which ganglia are affected and the extent of neuronal degeneration. This would allow us to identify and characterise any differences in pathology that might account for the differences in clinical signs. This would be a significant contribution towards determining if these dysautonomias are all induced by the same causal agent, and—if it is the same agent—shed light on how this causal agent spreads throughout the nervous system of these different species.

Another limitation of dysautonomia research to date is the lack of in vitro models for testing suspected causal agents in veterinary species. Generation of advanced tissue culture models consisting of appropriate cell types, such as organoids with neuronal co‐culture or organ‐on‐a‐chip models capturing ganglionic neuronal interactions,
106
, 
107
 would offer species‐relevant methods for testing suspected causal agents. While organoid models have been developed for some veterinary species,
108
, 
109
, 
110
, 
111
 there is currently no model that includes a neuronal element to capture neuronal damage, which is a key feature of dysautonomia. Organoid models of the GI tract with a neuronal component have been developed for people
112
, 
113
; however, these were derived from pluripotent stem cells rather than primary tissue and therefore do not contain the epigenetic stamp associated with primary tissue, making them a less accurate representation of naturally occurring responses than organoids derived from primary tissue. If a single causal agent could be identified, isolated and proven to be the cause of dysautonomia in each of the veterinary species, this would provide a starting point for researchers to develop targeted therapeutic and preventative treatments. Species‐relevant models could also be used for preliminary toxicity testing of therapeutic compounds or vaccines. Therefore, financial investment in the development of existing and novel models is vital to unlock the potential for rapid and safe screening of candidate causative agents and therapeutics.

title: Exploring the Effects of Pemivibart Monoclonal Antibody Infusion in Long COVID: A Case Series Offering Initial Clinical Insights.
clinical_text:
[ABSTRACT]
Long COVID, or post-COVID conditions (PCC), affects a substantial proportion of adults and is characterized by persistent symptoms such as fatigue, postexertional malaise (PEM), cognitive dysfunction, and dysautonomia. At present, no Food and Drug Administration-approved therapies exist. Pemivibart (Pemgarda), a monoclonal antibody (mAb) authorized under Emergency Use Authorization (EUA) for preexposure prophylaxis in immunocompromised individuals, has not been studied for PCC but may theoretically facilitate clearance of viral antigens.We report three individuals with longstanding, debilitating PCC who received pemivibart infusion under EUA. Each experienced rapid symptomatic improvement, most notably in fatigue with PEM, dysautonomia, and cognitive dysfunction. One patient achieved resolution of her most limiting symptoms within a week and sustained functional recovery following repeat infusion. Another demonstrated significant gains across several symptom domains and was able to resume prior physical activities, although benefits waned after two to three weeks. A third with autoimmune comorbidities reported dramatic improvement in energy and cognition, and continued to feel well at six weeks.The rationale for this case series stems from emerging hypotheses that persistent viral antigens may contribute to the pathophysiology of Long COVID and that neutralizing antibodies could facilitate antigen clearance and symptom resolution. In the three cases, pemivibart infusion was temporally associated with rapid and meaningful improvement in fatigue associated with PEM, cognitive dysfunction, and dysautonomia, symptom clusters that often drive functional impairment in PCC. While the magnitude and duration of benefit varied among individuals, the consistent pattern of improvement supports further exploration of mAb therapy as a potential disease-modifying approach. These preliminary findings highlight the need for controlled, biomarker-guided studies to determine efficacy, durability, and patient subgroups most likely to respond. Pemivibart remains authorized only for preexposure prophylaxis in immunocompromised individuals and is not approved for the treatment of PCC.

---

[CASE PRESENTATION]
Case 1

In April 2024, a 70-year-old woman with a history of numerous allergies, including an allergic response to the Moderna COVID-19 vaccine (Moderna, Inc., Cambridge, Massachusetts), developed severe COVID-19 with significant dyspnea. After resolution of the initial infection, she experienced ongoing breathlessness, along with PEM, dysautonomia, digestive issues, syncopal episodes, and intermittent cognitive fog. Workup with her pulmonologist, including pulmonary function testing, was unrevealing, other than mildly reduced diffusing capacity (Table 1). Symptoms were felt to be related to Long COVID.

FVC: forced vital capacity; FEV₁: forced expiratory volume in one second; FEV₁/FVC: ratio of forced expiratory volume in one second to forced vital capacity; TLC: total lung capacity; RV: residual volume; DLCO: diffusing capacity for carbon monoxide; DL/VA: diffusing capacity per unit alveolar volume; pre: prebronchodilator measurement; post: postbronchodilator measurement; % pred: percent predicted

Her symptoms progressively worsened over the next few months, with PEM becoming her most debilitating symptom. Before her initial infection, she reported being very physically active, regularly running 3 miles/day. Following COVID-19 and the development of PCC, she was unable to participate in even mild household activities due to severe "crashes” characterized by flaring of PCC symptoms, particularly fatigue. Additionally, she reported experiencing palpitations nearly constantly and developed syncopal episodes on multiple occasions. Diagnostic evaluation, including basic blood work, inflammatory markers, and rheumatologic screening, was unremarkable. She attempted various methods for symptomatic management, both pharmacologic and nonpharmacologic, including low-dose naltrexone, N-acetylcysteine, physical/occupational therapy, breathwork, yoga, and increased salt intake, but none provided durable relief for the symptom constellation.

Due to a history of severe COVID-19 with an inability to take vaccination, she was provided pemivibart infusion for preexposure prophylaxis in February 2025. Over the subsequent several days, the patient reported a dramatic improvement in numerous PCC symptoms. Brain fog and dysautonomia resolved within three days of the infusion, and her PEM resolved within one week. At follow-up two months later, she continued to report a complete resolution of PEM, dysautonomia, and brain fog, and was able to engage in moderate physical activity (weightlifting, tai chi, running) and resume writing a book without issue. In early April, she experienced two episodes of near syncope and palpitations similar to those she experienced before the infusion. The patient received a second pemivibart infusion in July 2025. Within two weeks, she reported further improvement to the PCC, with her cardiologist noting that dysautonomia symptoms "remarkably improved after receiving an infusion of mAbs.”

Case 2

In August 2021, a 63-year-old man developed COVID-19 with symptoms of fever, cough, dyspnea, myalgias, arthralgias, anosmia, and dysgeusia. He was treated with oral steroids and azithromycin in an outpatient setting. After the initial infection, he experienced a myriad of symptoms, including chronic fatigue, PEM, brain fog, dyspnea, arthralgias and muscle pain, paresthesias, headaches, muscle twitching, and depression/anxiety exacerbation. Over the following years, medical evaluation was suggestive of psoriatic arthritis, and his rheumatologist started him on methotrexate.

While his general symptom constellation waxed and waned, it progressively worsened overall, significantly decreasing his function and quality of life. His most bothersome symptoms were fatigue with PEM, generalized pain, occipital headaches, and brain fog. During his postexertional crashes, he experienced daily low-grade fevers, muscle twitching, tremors, headaches, and debilitating fatigue and brain fog. These symptoms caused him to reduce his activity significantly; before the infection, he was very physically active, completing projects in the yard and around the house, but now he was so fatigued that he needed to sit for most of the day and required assistance with instrumental activities of daily living. He acknowledged that this also took a toll on him emotionally, stating he was “half the man (he) used to be.” Medical treatment included low-dose naltrexone and bupropion, both of which were ineffective.

Due to immunosuppression in the setting of medical treatment of psoriatic arthritis, he was provided pemivibart infusion for preexposure prophylaxis in April 2025. The patient noted substantial improvement in his PCC shortly after the infusion. In the first week after the infusion, he did not experience any postexertional crashes and was able to resume some of his old activities, including wood chopping. Patient-Reported Outcomes Measurement Information System-29 (PROMIS-29) scoring performed pre- and postinfusion indicated improvement across several domains, including physical function, anxiety/depression, fatigue, sleep, social function, and pain (Table 2). The patient noted that his benefits persisted for 2.5 weeks, until the fatigue, headaches, fevers, and joint pain returned. He expressed eagerness for repeat infusion in the future.

PROMIS-29: Patient-Reported Outcomes Measurement Information System-29

Case 3

In May 2021, a 57-year-old woman with a complex medical history, including asthma, insomnia, chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy, and Sjogren’s syndrome, developed COVID-19. During the infection, she experienced worsening lower extremity numbness, and she was hospitalized for a persistent sore throat with fevers for a month. She completed the Pfizer COVID-19 vaccine course in September 2021, after which she experienced gastroparesis with irritable bowel syndrome symptoms.

Long COVID symptoms, which developed subsequent to the initial illness, included severe fatigue and PEM, exertional dyspnea, dysautonomia, sleep disturbances, chest pain, brain fog, and frequent migraines. Over the following years, she attempted various medication treatments for the condition including ivermectin, along with multiple supplements such as alpha lipoic acid, bromelain, dandelion, ginger root, magnesium glycinate, N-acetylcysteine, nattokinase, omega-3 fatty acids, a multivitamin, probiotics, resveratrol, selenium, turmeric, vitamin B12, vitamin C, vitamin D3, vitamin E, vitamin K2, and zinc. At the time of presentation to our clinic in June 2025, fatigue with PEM and sleep disturbances continued to significantly disrupt her daily function and overall quality of life.

Due to immunosuppression in the setting of hydroxychloroquine use for autoimmune disease, she was provided with pemivibart infusion for preexposure prophylaxis in August 2025. On the first day after the infusion, she experienced a severe gastrointestinal reaction with generalized body pain, but she subsequently noticed a significant improvement in her symptoms. Over the coming days, she reported feeling “resurrected from the dead,” citing dramatically improved energy and cognitive function. Before the infusion, she had been unable to participate in even mild activities due to PEM, but afterward, she became able to walk on the treadmill and socialize with friends without crashing. Following the infusion, she was noted to have an improvement on the DePaul Symptom Questionnaire-Short Form (DSQ-SF) from 40/40 to 4/40, indicating substantial improvement in symptom constellation (Table 3). At a follow-up visit six weeks after infusion, she noted that her only residual symptom in the weeks following the infusion was ongoing sleep dysregulation. She reported she continued to feel the benefits of the infusion, stating, “I am still doing incredible.”

DSQ-SF: DePaul Symptom Questionnaire-Short Form

---

[DISCUSSION]
This case series examined the potential clinical effects of pemivibart, a SARS-CoV-2-neutralizing mAb, in individuals with Long COVID. Three patients with longstanding, debilitating symptoms experienced rapid and meaningful improvement following administration. Across the cases, the most striking benefits were resolution or attenuation of fatigue with PEM, cognitive dysfunction, and dysautonomia, symptom clusters strongly associated with loss of function in PCC [1,2]. Improvements were not only subjectively reported but also reflected in functional outcomes, including resumption of prior physical activities and improved patient-reported outcome scores (e.g., PROMIS-29, DSQ-SF). The temporal relationship between infusion and symptomatic improvement, followed by eventual waning in some cases, suggests a treatment effect rather than spontaneous fluctuation, although placebo and regression-to-the-mean effects cannot be excluded.

The observed improvements are biologically plausible within current mechanistic models of Long COVID. Persistent viral antigens have been identified in plasma and tissue samples months after infection, raising the possibility that ongoing immune activation is perpetuated by residual viral material [7,8]. mAbs against SARS-CoV-2, such as pemivibart, are designed to neutralize circulating virus and promote viral clearance. By reducing antigen burden, mAbs could attenuate downstream immune dysregulation, microvascular dysfunction, or neuroinflammation, processes increasingly implicated in PEM, dysautonomia, and cognitive impairment [6,13].

These cases build upon emerging but limited literature, suggesting the potential benefit of mAb therapy in PCC. In a 2024 case series, Scheppke et al. described individuals with severe, persistent post-COVID symptoms who experienced marked improvement following mAb infusions, including remission of fatigue and cognitive complaints [11]. More recently, a blinded, placebo-controlled trial led by Peluso at the University of California, San Francisco, tested mAb AER002 in 36 patients with Long COVID (Website: Spring 2025 symposium - PolyBio Research Foundation; 2025). While the study results are not yet published, early data presentation indicates that no significant difference in symptom improvement across outcome measures (PROMIS-29, C-reactive protein, interleukin-6) was observed between the antibody and placebo arms, though the treatment was well tolerated and provides critical insight for future trial design.

Divergent findings from prior reports and the present case series highlight both the heterogeneity of response and the need for biomarker-guided approaches to identify the patient subgroups who are most likely to benefit (Website: Spring 2025 symposium - PolyBio Research Foundation; 2025) [11]. In this series, one patient experienced sustained remission of PEM and cognitive symptoms for nearly two months, while another experienced improvements lasting less than three weeks. The third reported dramatic symptomatic relief despite an initial infusion-related adverse reaction. This variability may reflect differences in underlying pathophysiology, comorbid conditions, or host-virus interactions. Identifying biomarkers predictive of response will be critical for guiding future trials and patient selection.

Several limitations are noted in the present report. First, these are uncontrolled case observations without blinded assessments, and natural fluctuation of the illness or placebo effects cannot be excluded. Second, symptom reporting relied on patient accounts, though in two cases, validated patient-reported outcome tools were also employed. Finally, the generalizability of these observations is limited by small sample size, heterogeneity of prior infection, and variability in comorbidities.

Despite these limitations, the consistent and sometimes dramatic symptom improvements across distinct cases highlight mAbs as a potential therapeutic avenue for investigation in PCC. Future research should prioritize randomized, placebo-controlled trials to establish efficacy, optimal dosing intervals, and durability of benefit. Biomarker-driven studies may clarify whether subsets of patients, such as those with evidence of persistent viral antigen, derive particular improvement.

Importantly, pemivibart is currently available only under EUA for preexposure prophylaxis in immunocompromised individuals and is not FDA-approved for the treatment of COVID-19 or Long COVID. Its use in the three cases presented was for preexposure prophylaxis, consistent with EUA guidance, and results should be interpreted with caution. Nevertheless, these cases contribute to a growing body of evidence that targeting viral persistence with neutralizing antibodies may offer relief for some patients with Long COVID, and they underscore the urgent need for systematic investigation of targeted biologic therapies in this population.

title: Cerebral fat embolism presenting as paroxysmal sympathetic hyperactivity.
clinical_text:
[ABSTRACT]
Traumatic injuries and procedures under anesthesia can both predispose patients to altered mental status for many reasons. In this case, a 21 year old man presented with an isolated femur fracture and developed paroxysmal sympathetic hyperactivity after surgical fixation. This case highlights the diagnostic considerations when a trauma patient develops dysautonomia and altered mental status and explores therapeutic options for treating a patient with sympathetic storming.

---

[TITLE]
Cerebral fat embolism presenting as paroxysmal sympathetic hyperactivity

---

[PRESENTATION]
The patient is a 21 year old male whose only past medical history was depression managed by a low dose SSRI who presented to the Emergency Department via EMS after a motor vehicle accident. The incident itself involved only the patient's vehicle, which had rolled over at high speed and resulted in a prolonged extrication of about 30 min. On arrival to the Emergency Department, he had an obvious deformity to the left femur with severe pain. He was neurovascularly intact throughout the injured extremity. After a comprehensive trauma evaluation, he was diagnosed with an isolated displaced proximal femoral diaphyseal fracture (Fig. 1). He was admitted to the Orthopedic Surgery service and approximately 8.5 h later his fracture was surgically repaired by intramedullary femoral nailing. The patient emerged smoothly from anesthesia and recovered for the next 3 h in the Post Anesthesia Care Unit. He had normal vital signs, was neurologically normal, and his pain was well controlled.Fig. 1The patient suffered a left midshaft femur fracture as a result of his motor vehicle accident.Fig. 1

The patient suffered a left midshaft femur fracture as a result of his motor vehicle accident.

Approximately 3.5 h after his surgery was complete, he developed a marked sinus tachycardia, with rates ranging from 130 to 170 beats per minute. He was mildly tachypneic, flushed, diaphoretic and tremulous, with a normal blood pressure and afebrile (oral temperature 98.4 F). He complained of chest pain, shortness of breath, and was not oriented to location or situation. The patient's surgical site was reexamined, and compartments were soft, without palpable hematomas or overlying ecchymosis. He required urethral catheterization for urinary retention and 600 cc urine was removed. An EKG demonstrated sinus tachycardia with a rightward axis. Pertinent laboratory evaluation included a high sensitivity troponin of 12 ng/L, and an elevated lactate at 9.2 mmol/L. He was administered a 1 L bolus of isotonic crystalloid and underwent emergent CT imaging with a non-contrast head CT, CT angiography of the head and neck, and a CT pulmonary angiogram. These studies were negative for intracranial hemorrhage, cerebral hypodensity, head or neck large vessel occlusion, evidence of fat embolism, or pulmonary emboli.

The patient was admitted to the Surgical Intensive Care Unit (SICU) for further diagnostics and stabilization. Over the next 24 h the patient remained somnolent with a persistent heart rate in the 130 beats per minute. When stimulated by voice or touch, he displayed a stereotypical paroxysm that included inconsolable moaning and crying, tachycardia up to the 180 beats per minute, bilateral pedal clonus and muscle rigidity, diaphoresis, tachypnea, and meiosis. Administration of benzodiazepines during these episodes appeared to have a variable effect but the episodes were ultimately self-limited and resolved after the patient was left undisturbed for several minutes. Repeated stimulation reliably induced this paroxysm. When the patient was not experiencing these episodes, he continued to be tachycardic to 130 beats per minute, and remained afebrile, somnolent and had normal muscle tone. Neurology was consulted to facilitate continuous EEG monitoring given a concern of non-convulsive seizures and he was loaded with 4 g of intravenous levetiracetam. Additionally, an MRI with and without gadolinium was performed (Fig. 2).Fig. 2MRI demonstrated multiple punctate hyperintensities scattered across the bilateral cortex on both DWI (left) and T2 FLAIR (right) imaging. Red arrows indicate the characteristic “starfield pattern” seen in cerebral fat emboli syndrome. (For interpretation of the references to colour in this figure legend, the reader is referred to the web version of this article.)Fig. 2

MRI demonstrated multiple punctate hyperintensities scattered across the bilateral cortex on both DWI (left) and T2 FLAIR (right) imaging. Red arrows indicate the characteristic “starfield pattern” seen in cerebral fat emboli syndrome. (For interpretation of the references to colour in this figure legend, the reader is referred to the web version of this article.)

Several of these stereotyped events were observed while the patient was monitored with video EEG and they were not felt to represent ictal or interictal epileptic phenomena. There was abundant 1–2 Hz generalized rhythmic delta activity and periodic sharp discharges (GRDA + S) with a frontal predominance. These were felt to represent a non-specific sign of intracranial pathology. Ultimately, seizures were excluded based on 72 h of cvEEG monitoring.

The MRI was interpreted by a neuroradiologist as “innumerable punctate acute infarcts in the bilateral cerebral white matter, with…a few punctate cortical infarcts in the high right frontal lobe.” Given the patient's clinical presentation with the antecedent femur fracture repair, these infarcts were felt to be consistent with fat emboli. The patient underwent a transthoracic echocardiogram which was negative for intracardiac shunt.

Over the next week the patient's mental status slowly improved. He was evaluated by speech language pathology and gradually improved from moderate-severe cognitive-linguistic deficits to mild cognitive-linguistic deficits. He was discharged to inpatient rehabilitation for his physical needs but was determined not to need additional speech therapy. At a follow-up visit 10 days after discharge, he was noted to have returned to his neurologic and cognitive baseline.

---

[THE DIAGNOSIS AND TREATMENT]
This case represents the rare phenomenon of Paroxysmal Sympathetic Hyperactivity (PSH) syndrome secondary to cerebral fat embolism syndrome. Because of delayed recognition of PSH as a possible presentation of fat embolism syndrome, our patient never received many of the potential therapeutics that can treat this sympathetic storm. Fat embolism syndrome refers to pulmonary, cerebral, and hematologic effects of fat globules entering the circulation [1,2]. This typically occurs after long bone fractures and predominates in young males and when operative fixation is delayed [3]. Cerebral fat embolism syndrome is hypothesized to occur when globules of fat are introduced into the cerebral circulation via a cardiac shunt or transit across the pulmonary capillary bed and enter the systemic circulation as microemboli [1,2]. This results in a shower of microemboli and leads to a “starfield pattern” on MRI [[4], [5], [6]].

The presentation of fat embolism syndrome is incredibly varied and can involve a progressive decline in mental status, stroke-like symptoms, seizures, and/or autonomic dysfunction [1,2]. Classically, “fat embolism syndrome” refers to a classic triad of neurologic disturbances, respiratory compromise, and petechial rash, though the incidence of all three in patients with clinically significant fat embolism is thought to be rare. Our patient presented with autonomic dysfunction from sympathetic storming, making the diagnosis less clear until further evidence was provided by MRI.

PSH is a poorly understood phenomenon in which patients exhibit paroxysmal excessive sympathetic nervous system activation in the setting of a cerebral insult [7,8]. While the majority of PSH cases in the literature are associated with traumatic brain injuries (TBIs), we have identified only five published cases describing PSH as a result of cerebral fat embolism syndrome [[9], [10], [11]]. In the setting of TBI, PSH most often presents after one week from the initial trauma [7]. In contrast, in both our and the five additional patients described in case reports, symptoms began within 24 h after the patient's fracture and in the absence of prior clinical and radiographically identifiable intracranial injury. Additionally, while PSH is associated with poor prognosis when it presents in patients with TBI, we note that in the relatively limited case reports of PSH secondary to fat embolism syndrome patients tend to have favorable neurologic recovery.

Care for patients experiencing PSH is generally preventative (ie. avoiding triggers) and supportive with pharmacologic adjuncts to reduce downstream effects of the sympathetic storm. To date there are no randomized clinical trials for the treatment of PSH, though various pilot studies, case reports, and observational studies recommend benzodiazepines, propofol, opioids beta blockade (specifically propranolol), and dexmedetomidine as reasonable options. Benzodiazepines and propofol act on central GABA receptors to directly quell electrical storming [7,12]. Benzodiazepines have the clear advantage that they can be used in non-ventilated patients, though respiratory depression is still a concern. Opioids act on the μ-opioid receptor, blocking the pathways that are thought to be responsible for autonomic dysfunction. Both benzodiazepines and opioids are generally described in their use as abortives of acute PSH episodes and evidence is lacking as to whether continuous infusions or scheduled doses may have a role in prevention. Propranolol, a non-selective β-blocker with central effects, has long been a mainstay for symptomatic treatment of patients with severe TBIs. There is some evidence to suggest a mortality benefit of propranolol in this population in comparison to other β-blockers [13,14]. This benefit is thought to derive from non-selectivity of propranolol and its lipophilicity, which allows it to more readily act centrally. Propranolol is hypothesized to block the effects of the catecholamine surge of PSH, primarily treating resultant hypertension and tachycardia [12]. Similarly, dexmedetomidine, an α2-agonist, acts on central receptors to block the release of norepinephrine and reduce sympathetic outflow [12]. Dexmedetomidine as a continuous infusion is a frequently used medication in the ICU setting and is one of the few treatments that has been described as a possible preventative for PSH episodes.

There is no evidence to suggest clear superiority of one pharmacologic strategy over another and the treatment of PSH generally involves a combination of medications to act on the cause as well as the effects of catecholamine surges. Furthermore, given that studies of patients with PSH are almost exclusively done in patients suffering severe TBIs, it is unclear to what extent this evidence applies to patients with PSH secondary to cerebral fat embolism syndrome.

---

[CONCLUSION]
While physicians should continue to keep cerebral fat embolism syndrome on their differential in cases where a patient with long bone injuries appears to display PSH, this should not overshadow concurrent workup to rule out neuroleptic malignant syndrome, malignant hyperthermia, serotonin syndrome, pulmonary emboli, seizures, and other entities that may present similarly and are in need of urgent and targeted treatment.

---

[GLOSSARY]

fat embolism syndrome

paroxysmal sympathetic hyperactivity

traumatic brain injury

No funding was provided for this manuscript.

title: Autoimmune Epilepsy Secondary to CASPR2 Antibody Encephalitis: A Case Report Highlighting Diagnostic Challenges and Management.
clinical_text:
[ABSTRACT]
CASPR2 (contactin-associated protein-like 2) is a cell adhesion molecule expressed in both the central and peripheral nervous systems. CASPR2 autoantibodies are associated with autoimmune encephalitis and epilepsy; however, the initial presentation and subsequent treatment can be challenging. We report a rare case of CASPR2-related new-onset seizures, culminating in a motor vehicle accident, as well as dysautonomia in a 50-year-old man with a prior history of vasovagal syncope. The patient experienced three types of seizures: (i) focal preserved consciousness seizures, (ii) focal preserved consciousness seizures/dysautonomia, and (iii) focal impaired consciousness seizures. Post-ictal confusion included stripping clothes off due to feeling hot. Video electroencephalogram (EEG) monitoring confirmed bilateral temporal lobe seizures. Further evaluation revealed anti-CASPR2 antibody positivity in both serum and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), consistent with autoimmune epilepsy. Despite treatment with intravenous (IV) methylprednisolone (1 g/day for five days) and multiple antiseizure medications (levetiracetam, lacosamide, and oxcarbazepine), the patient experienced persistent recurrent seizures, cognitive deficits, and medication-related side effects. This prompted adding IV immunoglobulin therapy, which helped with seizure control. This case underscores the diagnostic challenges of CASPR2 autoimmune epilepsy and highlights the importance of early recognition and treatment.

---

[CASE PRESENTATION]
A 50-year-old male construction company owner with a long-standing history of vasovagal syncope, averaging one episode annually, presented with new-onset spells of dizziness, staring, and unresponsiveness beginning in January 2024. Initially misdiagnosed as syncope, these episodes progressively increased in frequency, culminating in a motor vehicle accident on November 25, 2024. During this accident, the patient swerved across four lanes of traffic, striking another vehicle. Although airbags deployed, it remains uncertain whether he sustained a head injury. The patient has no recollection of exiting the vehicle and was found by EMS walking alongside the highway. He was admitted to the hospital from November 25 to November 28, 2024. While in the emergency department, he experienced a seizure characterized by staring, unresponsiveness, and nonsensical speech lasting two minutes, without abnormal jerking movements.

The patient's past medical history includes vasovagal syncope since age 10, with no prior history of head trauma, meningitis, or encephalitis. Family history is notable for malignancy, with a paternal first cousin and maternal aunt succumbing to cancer; however, no epilepsy or autoimmune disorders have been reported. Social history reveals he is a former smoker, having quit over 20 years ago, and he has no history of alcohol abuse. The initial diagnostic workup, summarized in Table 1, was unremarkable and included a complete blood count (CBC), basic metabolic panel (BMP), liver function tests (LFTs), lipase, lactic acid, an alcohol/drug screen, a non-contrast head CT scan, and a head/neck CT angiography. Additionally, the brain MRI, both with and without contrast, during hospitalization, was unremarkable.

*Autoimmune epilepsy antibody panel includes CASPR2 (contactin-associated protein-like 2), GAD65 (glutamic acid decarboxylase 65), VGKC (voltage-gated potassium channel), LGI1 (leucine-rich glioma-inactivated 1), and NR1 (NR1 subunit of the N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) receptor) antibodies.

WBC: white blood cells; RBC: red blood cells; BUN: blood urea nitrogen; AST: aspartate aminotransferase; ALT: alanine aminotransferase.

Given suspicion of seizure activity, levetiracetam 750 mg orally twice daily was initiated during hospitalization. Long-term EEG monitoring revealed focal epileptic seizures characterized by rhythmic 2-3 Hz activity at the T4 region, evolving into higher amplitude, slowing to 1 Hz, and abruptly ceasing after 40 seconds (Figure 1). Consequently, levetiracetam was increased to 1000 mg orally twice daily. Subsequent 24-hour EEG monitoring showed no electrographic seizures, and the patient was discharged on this regimen with follow-up scheduled at the epilepsy clinic.

Red-line box: Seizure onset marked by rhythmic 3 Hz activity, most prominent at T4 and best visualized in the parasagittal chains. Blue-line box: Morphology changes with increased amplitude and sharply contoured waveforms. Purple-line box: Frequency decreases to 1.5–2 Hz.

During his follow-up visit on December 19, 2024, the patient reported three distinct seizure types: (i) Focal preserved consciousness seizures occurred three to four times daily, characterized by déjà vu, sweating, dizziness, and olfactory hallucinations (e.g., coffee scent), lasting 15-20 seconds. Notably, sweating and dizziness could also represent symptoms of dysautonomia in this case; (ii) focal preserved consciousness seizures/dysautonomia manifested as a numb feeling in the body that comes in waves, goosebumps, and light-headedness, occurring multiple times per day; and (iii) focal impaired consciousness seizures, occurring three to four times weekly, were typified by staring, unresponsiveness, nonsensical speech, and postictal confusion lasting several minutes. The patient also reported significant cognitive decline, including difficulties with work-related tasks, short-term memory deficits, challenges with facial recognition, trouble forming sentences, and difficulty understanding conversations. Additional symptoms included emotional lability, irritability, and insomnia. Vasovagal episodes, triggered by emotional stress (e.g., seeing blood), manifested as sweating, pallor, and transient loss of consciousness without postictal confusion. Generalized muscle twitching, involving the shoulders, glutes, and face, was reported but visually unconfirmed. Subsequently, lacosamide therapy was initiated at 50 mg orally twice daily, titrated to 150 mg twice daily.

The constellation of symptoms raised concern for an autoimmune or paraneoplastic process. Therefore, serum autoimmune encephalitis/paraneoplastic antibody panel testing was performed and revealed anti-CASPR2 antibody positivity (serum titer: 1:100), warranting hospital readmission from January 8 to 10, 2025, for further expedited management. Lumbar puncture results showed a protein level of 29 mg/dL, a glucose level of 75 mg/dL, and a CSF cell count of 4 cells/µL, with 95% lymphocytes (Table 2). Herpes Simplex Virus PCR testing was negative. The autoimmune antibody panel confirmed anti-CASPR2 antibody positivity (CSF titer: 1:160).

* The encephalitis/paraneoplastic autoantibody panel includes ANNA1 (HU), ANNA2 (RI), ANNA3, PCA1 (YO), PCA2, PCA TR (DNER), AGNA/SOX1 Glial nuclear type 1, Amphiphysin, CRMP5/CV2, GAD65, MA2/TA, Myelin, AQP4, NMDAR1, AMPAR1, AMPAR2, GABABR, LGI1, CASPR2, DPPX Receptor, and VGKC antibodies.

EEG monitoring during sleep revealed rhythmic activity buildup in the left temporal region, evolving over several seconds and lasting 30 seconds, without clinical correlation and suggestive of subclinical seizures. CT imaging of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis with contrast was negative for malignancy. The patient was treated with IV methylprednisolone 1 g daily for five days and discharged on January 10, 2025, with levetiracetam 1000 mg twice daily and lacosamide 200 mg twice daily. Further steroid therapy and consideration of other potential immunotherapy agents, such as IVIG, were deferred until his follow-up visit within three weeks of discharge.

Post-discharge, the patient remained seizure-free for approximately one month but later experienced breakthrough seizures, including episodes of confusion, automatisms, and postictal symptoms, such as unresponsiveness with lip smacking during a phone call. Oxcarbazepine 600 mg orally twice daily was added for seizure control. Despite treatment, cognitive deficits, emotional lability, and irritability persisted. The patient continued to experience generalized muscle twitching. To evaluate for CASPR2 antibody-associated peripheral nerve hyperexcitability syndrome, an electromyography (EMG) and nerve conduction study (NCS) were performed, with attention to findings such as increased insertional activity, myokymic discharges, fasciculations, and neuromyotonic discharges. However, the results were unremarkable, showing no evidence of large-fiber peripheral neuropathy, hyperexcitability, polyradiculopathy, or myopathy (Tables 3, 4).

ADM: abductor digiti minimi; AHB: abductor hallucis; APB: abductor pollicis brevis; EDB: extensor digitorum brevis; NL: normal.

Fasc: fasciculation potentials; FDI: first dorsal interosseous; Fibs: fibrillation potentials; NL: normal; Poly: polyphasic; PSW: positive sharp waves; Recrt: recruitment; Spon Disc: spontaneous discharges.

The follow-up plan included a 12-week course of IV methylprednisolone (1 g weekly for six weeks, starting at the end of January 2025, then biweekly for six weeks) and IVIG therapy (a total of 2 g/kg administered over three days from March 12 to 14, 2025). Overall, this immunotherapy strategy was selected based on emerging evidence and consensus guidelines for CASPR2 antibody-associated autoimmune encephalitis [12,13]. Subsequently, IVIG was planned at 0.5 g/kg every six weeks, with continued methylprednisolone therapy for seven additional weeks. Adjustments were based on therapeutic response. Antiseizure medication doses were modified to levetiracetam 1500 mg twice daily, lacosamide 200 mg twice daily, and oxcarbazepine 300 mg in the morning and 600 mg in the evening. These changes resulted in seizure freedom during the follow-up visit in May 2025.

Additionally, the patient underwent formal neuropsychological testing in late May 2025, which revealed intact baseline intellectual abilities and generally strong performance across most cognitive domains, including basic attention and working memory, executive functions (including cognitive flexibility, inhibition, and planning), confrontation and auditory naming, verbal fluency, and visuospatial skills. However, he showed broadly reduced encoding on memory tasks, with particular difficulty in retention and retrieval on verbal memory measures. Semantic fluency was notably weaker (average) compared to his high performance on phonemic fluency, and he exhibited an elevated number of repetition errors across verbal fluency trials. Overall, these deficits in verbal learning and memory, along with subtle vulnerability in semantic access efficiency, mainly suggest dysfunction in left temporal systems. Accordingly, the patient started cognitive rehabilitation therapy (to learn new compensatory strategies, particularly those aimed at supporting verbal learning and memory).

---

[DISCUSSION]
This case highlights the diagnostic challenges in distinguishing autoimmune epilepsy from other etiologies of seizures, particularly in patients presenting with a history of transient loss of consciousness or syncope. The identification of CASPR2 antibodies in both CSF and serum supported the diagnosis of autoimmune epilepsy. Notably, CASPR2 antibodies are more reliably identified in serum than in CSF, particularly in patients with peripheral nerve hyperexcitability syndromes [9,14,15]. While CSF positivity is highly specific for CNS involvement, such as limbic encephalitis, seizures, and cognitive impairment, serum testing offers greater sensitivity and should be prioritized in diagnostic evaluation [9,14]. Immunotherapy with IV corticosteroids led to a transient cessation of seizures in our case; however, the recurrence of breakthrough episodes and persistent cognitive deficits highlights the necessity for long-term immunological and neuropsychiatric management.

Autoantibodies targeting CASPR2 are associated with a spectrum of autoimmune neurological disorders. The most common clinical presentation is limbic encephalitis, characterized by subacute onset of memory impairment, confusion, mood disturbances, and seizures, often of temporal lobe origin [7,9,11,16,17]. These data also revealed that three (15%) CASPR2-IgG-seropositive patients with seizures exhibited coexisting PNS involvement. Of these, two patients demonstrated peripheral nerve hyperexcitability on electrodiagnostic studies, while one patient was diagnosed with small fiber neuropathy based on thermoregulatory sweat testing and autonomic reflex testing [17]. In our case, the first two (CNS features and autonomic instability) were predominant. Although the patient had a subjective feeling of generalized muscle twitching, the EMG/NCS did not find electrodiagnostic evidence of peripheral nerve hyperexcitability, including increased insertional activity, neuromyotonic discharges, myokymic discharges, and fasciculations.
